newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim warns Pyongyang against provocations.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim warns Pyongyang against provocations.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam said on Monday the defection of North Korea's top ideologue indicated a leadership shakeup in Pyongyang, and he warned the North that any provocation would bring ruin.

His comments to the Korea Military Academy followed reports that Northern soldiers again violated a ceasefire accord that ended the 1950-53 Korean War by intruding into the South Korean portion of a border buffer zone.

Foreign ministry officials said they expected a breakthrough this week in talks with China over the fate of the defector, holed up in a Seoul diplomatic mission in Beijing since seeking asylum there on February 12.
South Korea is seeking passage to Seoul for Hwang Jang-yop, chief architect of North Korea's ideology of Juche, a brand of fanatic self-reliance.
"The situation on the Korean peninsula is extremely unstable," Kim told a graduation ceremony at the academy.
"As the recent defecton of the theoretician of the so-called Juche idea demonstrates, serious changes are occurring in the North Korean ruling class right now."
He accused Pyongyang of making "frantic efforts" to launch a military lunge south while ignoring starving citizens.
"I strongly warn North Korea here and now that it would only bring its ruin if it commits a reckless provocation," Kim said.

In the past month, two of North Korea's most powerful military figures -- defence minister Choe Kwang and his deputy Kim Kwang-jin -- died while the prime minister was replaced, apparently for health reasons.
These and other changes in Pyongyang's secretive hierarchy have fuelled conspiracy theories in Seoul.

Some analysts believe North Korean leader Kim Jong-il is purging an ultra conservative old guard as he prepares to assume the posts of state president and head of the Worker's Party left vacant by the death in 1994 of his father, Kim Il-sung.

China has agonised over Hwang's fate, torn between an old socialist comrade and a new capitalist friend. Weeks of talks, interrupted by the death of paramount Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, have failed to settle the issue.
"I don't expect Hwang to leave Beijing this week but details of his departure will be discussed this week and could be worked out," said one foreign ministry official.
"Unlike previous discussions, talks this week will deal with Hwang's future in a package, including the method and the timing of his departure. A breakthrough is probable," he said.
Local media have speculated Beijing will release Hwang to a third country -- possibly Australia or Sweden -- on condition he stays there for a while before heading to South Korea.
South Korean foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said he believed Beijing would not send Hwang home.
Before dawn on Monday, five North Korean soldiers crossed into the southern half of the Demilitarized Zone for about 90 minutes, U.S. military spokesman Jim Coles said.
"While their presence in the area is a violation of the armistice agreement, they did not do anything provocative. It's rugged territory up there and it's easy to miss the line markers," he said.
The United States maintains 37,000 troops in South Korea and helps monitor the ceasefire.
A Seoul defence ministry official said such incursions were not unusual. "We are not very concerned," he said.
Last April, scores of North Korean troops carrying heavy weapons intruded on three occasions into the border crossing area of Panmunjom, sparking security concerns.
